research.query: What does a candle flame look like in microgravity?
research.answer:
The question was matched to: microgravity. Below is what the indexed documents state about it, quoted with their sources.

**Evidence**
- DAFT / DAFT-2: Dust can look like smoke to a particle counter. DAFT showed that a modified commercial particle counter could be used in microgravity, measuring a test dust aerosol released on the ISS. On the Moon, regolith dust will enter habitats: how will detectors discriminate dust from… [S1]
- ACME BRE: The key hypothesis is that the heat of combustion, smoke point, and heat of gasification of the fuel mixture will represent a real solid fuel (or liquid fuel absorbed in an inert matrix). Thus achieved steady burning would represent the potential for real solid fuels to… [S2]
- CFI: Flame combustion of liquid hydrocarbon fuels such as n-dodecane, n-dodecane/iso-dodecane mixtures, and faresane in microgravity can provide insights into low-temperature chemical kinetics, revealing critical parameters like droplet extinction diameters and flame dynamics that… [S3]
- BASS: Current NASA spacecraft materials selection is based on a standard test method (NASA–STD–6001 Test 1) that segregates material based on 1-g behavior without consideration of low gravity effects. A critical element of this understanding is the radiative heat emission from the… [S4]
- ACME/Flame Design: ACME/Flame Design Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design. Flames of Gaseous Fuels. Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME), Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), Reconfiguration of Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) [S5]
- Dust can look like smoke to a particle counter: DAFT showed that a modified commercial particle counter could be used in microgravity, measuring a test dust aerosol released on the ISS. Limitation: Terrestrial test dust, not lunar regolith; feasibility test only. [S10]
- BASS-II maps solid-fuel burning down to 13.6 % O2: BASS-II ran 129 tests with initial O2 between 13.6 and 22.2 % vol, mostly on PMMA, SIBAL (cotton-fiberglass fabric), Nomex. Flow annotations record extinction in 15 tests, blow-off in 3 and no ignition in 1. Limitation: Outcome annotations  [S11]

sources.title: DAFT / DAFT-2 — Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test / Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test-2 — insight:daft-dust-vs-smoke
sources.text: Dust can look like smoke to a particle counter. DAFT showed that a modified commercial particle counter could be used in microgravity, measuring a test dust aerosol released on the ISS. On the Moon, regolith dust will enter habitats: how will detectors discriminate dust from smoke to avoid nuisance alarms?

sources.title: ACME BRE — Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator — hypothesis
sources.text: The key hypothesis is that the heat of combustion, smoke point, and heat of gasification of the fuel mixture will represent a real solid fuel (or liquid fuel absorbed in an inert matrix). Thus achieved steady burning would represent the potential for real solid fuels to achieve steady burning in microgravity. Other than a candle flame, this has not been shown before.

sources.title: CFI — Cool Flames Investigation — hypothesis
sources.text: Flame combustion of liquid hydrocarbon fuels such as n-dodecane, n-dodecane/iso-dodecane mixtures, and faresane in microgravity can provide insights into low-temperature chemical kinetics, revealing critical parameters like droplet extinction diameters and flame dynamics that are not observable on Earth.

sources.title: BASS — Burning and Suppression of Solids — researchImpacts
sources.text: Current NASA spacecraft materials selection is based on a standard test method (NASA–STD–6001 Test 1) that segregates material based on 1-g behavior without consideration of low gravity effects. A critical element of this understanding is the radiative heat emission from the flame. These results are used in first order models and predictions of heat release in spacecraft fires and as a means to extend heat release data from tests like the NASA cone calorimeter test (NASA–STD–6001 Test 2) to a performance-based material selection process. Using nitrogen as a flame suppressant in microgravity provides a direct link to current and planned extinguishment techniques.

why: Strong text match with your question.

top_passage.text: The Saffire-1 experiments was performed on the Orbital Science’s Cygnus resupply vehicle after it deberthed from the ISS. The sample material for Saffire-I is a composite fabric called Sibal consisting of cotton on a fiberglass substrate (75% cotton, 25% fiberglass by weight). It has been used in many space experiments because it burns like cotton but maintains structural integrity after the cotton is consumed. The sample was approximately 0.94 meters long and 0.4 meters wide, simulating a large piece of flammable fabric. The Saffire-1 flight unit had a sample card installed in the middle of a large flow duct.

why: Data: 2 test-level records.

top_passage.text: The Saffire-I experiment provides a new way to study a realistic fire on an exploration vehicle, which has not been possible in the past because the risks are too high. Instruments on an unmanned cargo vessel measure oxygen, carbon dioxide, heat, pressure and flame growth, and two video cameras provide views of the flame. Results determine microgravity flammability limits for several spacecraft materials, help to validate NASA’s material selection criteria, and how microgravity and limited oxygen affect flame size. The investigation is crucial for the safety of current and future space missions.
